To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have improved the astrophysical reference frame in the Galactic Center by 2.5 times in position and 5 times in proper motion, and that the rotation of the previous astrometric frame has been removed.
we have measured the positions of seven infrared-bright SiO masers to a precision of 0.65 milli-arcsecond and proper motions of 0.3 milli-arcsecond/year.
we have improved the astrophysical reference frame within 15'' of the Galactic center by 2.5 times in position and 5 times in proper motion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the astrometry and dynamics of stars in close orbits about the supermassive object in our Galactic Center.
the astrophysics and astrometry of stars in the central parsec of the Galaxy.
the Galactic center and in particular with the dynamics of the central stellar cluster, and the supermassive object Sgr A*.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Galactic Center is a very good laboratory for testing general relativity.
the improved astrometric reference frames for the Galactic center have been developed and applied to the stellar orbits.
the improved astrometric reference frames have allowed us to measure the orbit of the star S2 to a precision of 0.3% (in the radial direction) and 0.6% (in the transverse direction).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have now reached the precision where we can detect the effects of general relativity.
we have improved the astrophysical precision of stellar orbits around Sgr A* by a factor of ~2.5.
we have made the most accurate astrometric reference for the inner few parsecs of our Galaxy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the astrometric frame is now sufficiently accurate to detect the effects of General Relativity on orbits of stars in the immediate vicinity of the black hole.

astrometric reference frames for the Galactic Center can be made more accurate than the reference frames that are used to measure orbits of extrasolar planets around nearby stars, and that the reference frames can be made more precise than the stellar orbits themselves, which will enable more accurate tests of General Relativity in the future.

we have improved the accuracy of the astrometric frame in which we are measuring orbits of stars near the Galactic Center by an order of magnitude, and have shown that it is possible to improve the frame by a similar factor in the next 5 years.
